q: In which case does a concurrence say speech and assembly are guaranteed against “the occasional tyranny of majorities”?
o: Whitney v. California
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Collin v. Smith
e: Whitney v. California (1927). Brandeis’s concurrence is read for values: counterspeech over coerced silence, and protection of the dissenting few.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Whitney v. California

q: In which case had the school board first required a “stiff-arm” salute that civic groups objected to as “too much like Hitler’s”?
o: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
Minersville School District v. Gobitis
e: Barnette (1943) was decided during World War II. The Court reasoned that the nation was fighting to protect exactly these freedoms.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

q: In which case had the employee already stopped locker-room prayers at his employer’s request before being disciplined for praying after three October games?
o: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
Mahmoud v. Taylor
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
e: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022). The district disciplined him for brief, quiet midfield prayers after the 2015 games.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Kennedy v. Bremerton School District

q: In which case did teacher guidance suggest calling a student’s objection “hurtful”?
o: Mahmoud v. Taylor
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Carson v. Makin
e: Mahmoud v. Taylor (2025). Correction of dissent was one reason the storybooks were a Yoder-type burden, not mere exposure.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Mahmoud v. Taylor

q: Which statement about Whitney v. California is accurate?
o: Its majority is no longer good law, but its concurrence states lasting values
Its majority is still good law for advocacy of crime by organized political groups
It was the first case to apply the Speech Clause to the states
It held criminal syndicalism laws void for vagueness as applied
e: Brandenburg v. Ohio overruled the majority in 1969. The casebook assigns the concurrence, not for a test, but for why speech is protected.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Whitney v. California

q: Which statement about West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette is accurate?
o: It treated the salute, a gesture, as a form of utterance
It barred schools from teaching students about the flag
It turned on how sincere the children’s religious beliefs were
It weighed the children’s rights against their classmates’ rights
e: Symbolic conduct is speech. Barnette noted no competing private rights were involved, only the authority of the state against the individual.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

q: Which statement about Kennedy v. Bremerton School District is accurate?
o: The Religion Clauses are complementary; the Establishment Clause doesn’t automatically win
The coach’s prayer was government speech that the school district was free to control
The district had to act to avoid an Establishment Clause violation, so its discipline stood
Public school employees give up their religious rights while they are on the job
e: The clauses share one sentence. The district’s Establishment Clause defense failed because the prayer wasn’t coercive.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Kennedy v. Bremerton School District

q: Which statement about Mahmoud v. Taylor is accurate?
o: It arose on a preliminary injunction, so it held the parents were likely to succeed
It ordered the county to remove the five storybooks from every classroom
It held that exposure to contrary ideas can never burden a family’s religious exercise
It overruled Smith for every law that touches public education
e: The parents sought opt-outs, not removal. The majority stressed they weren’t trying to micromanage the curriculum.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Mahmoud v. Taylor

q: How does the casebook’s gloss on Whitney tie “freedom to think” to all the First Amendment’s clauses?
o: No official church dictating belief, protection of belief, and peaceful tools for changing policy
A national church to unify belief, protected speech for its members, and a free press to report on it
Free speech for citizens only, with religion and assembly left for the states to regulate
Protection for spoken political ideas, but not for religious practice or symbolic conduct
e: Speech, assembly, and petition are the peaceful means of changing policy, so the Religion and Speech Clauses serve one theme.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Whitney v. California

q: What standard did Barnette say applies to restricting speech and worship?
o: They may be restricted only to prevent grave and immediate danger
They may be restricted whenever a rational basis supports the law
Speech may yield to wartime unity, but worship may never be restricted
Worship may yield to neutral laws, but compelled speech never may
e: Barnette rejected Gobitis’s deference to legislatures: fundamental rights don’t depend on the outcome of elections.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

q: Why did Kennedy say treating any visible religious conduct by a teacher as coercive would be a problem?
o: It would amount to hostility toward religion
It would make every school prayer case moot
It would require overruling Engel v. Vitale
It would put teachers under the Speech Clause
e: Tolerating others’ prayer is part of living in a pluralistic society. High schoolers can tell permission from endorsement.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Kennedy v. Bremerton School District

q: Why did Mahmoud say private school or homeschooling was no answer for the parents?
o: It is costly, and the parents already fund the public schools
Private schools in the county had refused to admit the children
Homeschooling was barred by state law for children under ten
The parents had no right to choose a religious education
e: Parental rights would be an “empty promise” if they stopped at the public school door (Pierce v. Society of Sisters).
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Mahmoud v. Taylor

q: Which era of incitement doctrine does the majority in Whitney v. California belong to?
o: 1919–27: clear and present danger or bad tendency
1949–51: clear and present danger of a serious substantive evil
1969 on: intent, imminence, and likelihood of lawless action
1942 on: personal insults likely to provoke an immediate fight
e: Whitney sits with Abrams, Schaefer, and Pierce. Terminiello and Dennis mark the middle era, and Brandenburg the modern one.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Whitney v. California

q: Which later case recast Barnette as an “especially egregious” example of coercion rather than the outer limit of protection?
o: Mahmoud v. Taylor
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
Wooley v. Maynard
Employment Division v. Smith
e: Mahmoud used this to reach beyond compelled affirmation. Its dissent read Barnette as protecting only against a compelled declaration.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

q: In the casebook’s comparison, how did the Kennedy majority’s facts differ from Mahmoud’s?
o: Older students and permitted private expression, not instruction of young children
A single school employee, not a county board acting through its full curriculum
A claimant of one faith, not parents from Muslim, Catholic, and Orthodox families together
A claim under federal law, not one brought under the state’s own constitution
e: The majorities stressed age, government instruction versus permitted private expression, and normative content versus passive observation.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Kennedy v. Bremerton School District

q: Which earlier case did Mahmoud cite for the parental right extending outside the home?
o: Pierce v. Society of Sisters
Wisconsin v. Yoder
Minersville School District v. Gobitis
Engel v. Vitale
e: Yoder supplied the type of burden; Pierce supplied the idea that parents’ rights reach education outside the home.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Mahmoud v. Taylor

q: A city council member proposes banning leaflets that urge, in general terms, overthrowing “the corrupt system” someday. Using the values in Brandeis’s Whitney concurrence and modern doctrine, what is the best response?
o: Answer the leaflets with more speech; general advocacy can’t be banned
Ban them, because the leaflets have a bad tendency to cause crime later
Ban them, if most voters approve the ban in a citywide referendum
Ban them, because Whitney’s majority upheld a law just like this one
e: The remedy for evil counsels is good ones. Today, general advocacy of force at some future time also fails Brandenburg’s intent, imminence, and likelihood elements.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Whitney v. California

q: A public middle school requires every student to sign a “patriotism pledge” card before joining any club. A student refuses for secular political reasons. What result?
o: The requirement violates the First Amendment under Barnette
It is valid, because the student’s objection isn’t religious
It is valid, because joining a club is only a privilege, not a right
It is valid, if the school also teaches the pledge’s history
e: A signed pledge is a confession of belief “by word or act.” The state may pursue unity by persuasion and example, not compulsion.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

q: A public high school math teacher bows her head silently before lunch in the cafeteria, where students can see her. The district disciplines her to avoid “endorsing” religion. What result under Kennedy?
o: The discipline likely violates Free Exercise; visible prayer isn’t coercion
The discipline is valid, because a reasonable observer would see endorsement
The discipline is valid, because teachers speak for the government all day
The discipline is valid under Lemon, because the district’s purpose was secular
e: Disciplining conduct because it is religious triggers strict scrutiny, and an Establishment Clause defense fails without coercion.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Kennedy v. Bremerton School District

q: A district adds a mandatory third-grade unit in which teachers read stories presenting one family structure as “the right way to live” and correct students who disagree. It keeps opt-outs for other units but denies them here. Religious parents sue. Best answer?
o: Opt-outs are likely required: a Yoder-type burden, undercut by other opt-outs
No opt-outs: the unit is neutral and generally applicable, so Smith controls
No opt-outs: parents who object to the curriculum may enroll in a private school
Opt-outs are required, and the unit must also be removed for every student
e: Normative content, young children, trusted teachers, and correction of dissent track Mahmoud’s burden. Strict scrutiny then applies.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Mahmoud v. Taylor

q: Which clauses make up the First Amendment?
o: Establishment, Free Exercise, Speech, Press, Assembly, and Petition
Speech, Press, Due Process, and Equal Protection
Establishment, Free Exercise, Speech, Press, and Freedom from Searches
Speech, Press, Religion, and the Right to Bear Arms
e: Assembly and Petition largely overlap with speech; the casebook treats the Press Clause as giving the press the same rights as everyone.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Scope of the First Amendment

q: How does the casebook treat the Press Clause?
o: As giving the press the same rights as everyone
As giving reporters a privilege to refuse subpoenas
As protecting only licensed newspapers
As covering only political reporting
e: That is why the Pentagon Papers case turns on prior-restraint doctrine that protects any speaker.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Scope of the First Amendment

q: What does it mean that the First Amendment is “not absolute”?
o: Fraud and falsely shouting fire can be punished; values are weighed against harms
Any speech may be restricted if a legislature finds a rational basis for the restriction
Speech is protected only when it concerns politics or religion
Courts must defer to the government during any declared emergency
e: The theme: freedom to think as you will and to speak as you think, with a small set of narrow exceptions.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Scope of the First Amendment

q: In the coercion synthesis, how did the Kennedy dissent view the coach’s prayer?
o: As coercive: demonstrative prayer at a school event by a coach who led players
As harmless: quiet personal prayer that no student could even have noticed
As government speech: the district had to adopt or forbid it
As a hybrid-rights case pairing religion with free speech
e: The majority saw brief, private prayer with no evidence of pressure; the dissent saw a long practice of 50-yard-line prayers.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — The coercion spectrum

q: In the coercion synthesis, how did the Mahmoud dissent view the storybooks?
o: As mere exposure, with no compelled declaration of belief
As coercion, but justified by the board’s compelling interest
As a Barnette-style compelled pledge by young students
As government endorsement of religion in the classroom
e: The dissent read Barnette as protecting only against compelled declarations, and Kennedy as holding exposure isn’t coercion.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — The coercion spectrum

q: A private social media company deletes a user’s political post. The user sues the company under the First Amendment. What result?
o: The user loses: private actors aren’t bound by the First Amendment
The user wins: political speech is the very core of the First Amendment
The user wins: a large platform is a public forum by its nature
The user loses, but only if the deleted post was false
e: The First Amendment binds federal, state, and local governments through incorporation, not private companies.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — Scope of the First Amendment

q: A state law requires all public employees to attend a one-hour training explaining the state’s diversity policies. Employees aren’t asked to agree with anything. An employee objects on religious grounds. Which case gives the state its strongest point?
o: Barnette: the state may explain its views so long as it doesn’t compel belief
Mahmoud: any exposure to contrary ideas is a burden on an employee’s religious exercise
Wooley: the employee must display the policy on her own property
Smith: the training is unconstitutional because it isn’t neutral
e: Barnette lets the state teach and acquaint people with its views; what it forbids is compelling a declaration. Adults, not young children, also cut against a Mahmoud burden.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment Overview — The coercion spectrum

q: Which case cited Reynolds (polygamy), Prince (child labor), Braunfeld (Sunday closing), and Gillette (draft) to support enforcing neutral laws against religious objectors?
o: Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Carson v. Makin
e: Smith (1990) read those cases as enforcing general laws despite religious objections, and explained the exemption cases as hybrid-rights cases.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: In which case did the Court say religious beliefs need not be “acceptable, logical, consistent, or comprehensible to others”?
o: Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
Employment Division v. Smith
Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
e: Lukumi (1993). The Santeria practice of animal sacrifice was protected religious exercise even if outsiders found it strange.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: In which case did a commissioner say the claimant could believe what he wanted but couldn’t act on those beliefs in business, and no one objected?
o: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
e: Masterpiece Cakeshop (2018). Other remarks compared religious justification to defenses of slavery and the Holocaust.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: In which case did the government’s interests in more foster parents, avoiding liability, and equal treatment all fail as applied to one agency?
o: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Carson v. Makin
Tandon v. Newsom
e: Fulton (2021). The agency added foster parents, the liability fear was speculative, and the city’s own exemption system undercut equal treatment.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: Which case was the fifth time the Court summarily rejected the Ninth Circuit on California’s COVID limits on worship?
o: Tandon v. Newsom
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Carson v. Makin
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
e: Tandon v. Newsom (2021), decided on an application for an injunction pending appeal.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: In which case did a state’s “nonsectarian” requirement, in place since 1981, apply to families in districts without a public secondary school?
o: Carson v. Makin
Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue
Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer
Mahmoud v. Taylor
e: Carson v. Makin (2022), from Maine. Espinoza involved a tax-credit scholarship and Trinity Lutheran a playground grant.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: Which statement about Employment Division v. Smith is accurate?
o: Belief is absolutely protected; conduct is protected only from laws targeting it as religious
Every substantial burden on religious conduct triggers strict scrutiny unless Congress says otherwise
Sacramental peyote use was exempt because the ritual was sincere and central
Its rule applies only to criminal laws, not to civil regulations like licensing
e: Smith denied the exemption from Oregon’s drug law. Strict scrutiny returned only by statute, through RFRA.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: Which statement about Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah is accurate?
o: The ordinances were underinclusive for both animal cruelty and public health
The ordinances were valid, because animal cruelty laws are neutral by their nature
The ordinances got rational basis, because they never named any religion
The ordinances were valid as emergency measures passed after a lease
e: A law can target religion without naming it. Exemptions for comparable secular killings showed the targeting.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: Which statement about Masterpiece Cakeshop is accurate?
o: It was narrow; states can generally protect gay persons’ equal access to goods
It gave bakers a free-speech right to refuse any wedding cake they disapprove of
It held Colorado’s antidiscrimination law facially invalid as applied to shops
It held a vendor’s sincere belief always outweighs a customer’s equal rights
e: The Court set aside the order for hostility and left the larger clash between antidiscrimination law and the First Amendment unresolved.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: Which statement about Fulton v. City of Philadelphia is accurate?
o: The Court ruled for the agency without overruling Smith
The Court overruled Smith and returned to case-by-case balancing
The Court held the referral policy neutral and generally applicable
The Court ordered the city to certify only the agency’s chosen families
e: The case turned on the contract’s discretionary exemption system, which made the policy not generally applicable.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: Which statement about Tandon v. Newsom is accurate?
o: It granted an injunction pending appeal; losing free exercise even briefly is irreparable
It upheld the limits, accepting the district court’s finding that homes were the riskier setting
It held that worship at home gets less protection than worship in a church building
It held that pandemic rules get rational basis review as emergency health measures
e: Losing free exercise rights “for even minimal periods of time” is irreparable harm.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: Which statement about Carson v. Makin is accurate?
o: The exclusion failed even though the money would pay for religious instruction
The exclusion survived because the money would pay for religious instruction
Every state must now fund religious schools, whether or not it funds private ones
The tuition program was a public-education benefit Maine could keep secular
e: Carson went past Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza on use: what the money buys doesn’t matter once the state subsidizes private schools.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: Why did Smith say Barnette didn’t help religious claimants seeking exemptions from neutral laws?
o: Barnette was really a speech case, decided on free-speech grounds
Barnette had been limited to wartime by later decisions
Barnette involved a federal law rather than a state law
Barnette protected adults, while Smith involved schoolchildren and parents
e: Smith used Barnette and Yoder as hybrid-rights examples: religion paired with speech or parental rights.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: Why were the Lukumi ordinances underinclusive as animal cruelty laws?
o: Fishing, pest extermination, euthanasia, research, and hunting were allowed
The city banned advertising sacrifices but never banned the sacrifices themselves
Cruelty laws can never reach religious rituals of any kind
The penalties were too small to deter anyone from killing animals
e: The public-health rationale failed the same way: hunters’ carcasses and restaurant garbage posed the same risks but were unregulated.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: Why was the commission’s hostility enough to set aside its order without resolving the larger conflict?
o: The claimant was owed neutral treatment, and a hostile hearing denied it
The hostility proved the law itself was not generally applicable on its face
The hostility showed that the couple had suffered no real injury
The commission lacked jurisdiction over bakeries in the first place
e: Even a neutral law must be applied neutrally. The unequal treatment of three other bakers confirmed the problem.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: Why did the city’s interest in avoiding liability fail in Fulton?
o: It was speculative
It wasn’t a legitimate government interest
The city had waived its immunity by contract
Courts never weigh liability in strict scrutiny
e: Strict scrutiny asks about the interest in denying this claimant an exemption, and a speculative risk doesn’t meet that burden.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: What did the Tandon dissent say the district court had found about at-home gatherings?
o: Homes were riskier: longer interactions, smaller spaces, and less masking
Homes were safer than stores, so the state had treated worship too harshly
Homes and salons posed identical risks under every precaution studied
No evidence existed either way, so the state could choose either rule
e: The dissent called the comparison to salons “apples and watermelons” and said at-home secular gatherings were the right comparator.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: According to Carson, what options did Maine still have?
o: Expand public schools, add busing or tutoring, or run its own boarding schools
Fund only those religious schools that agree to adopt the state curriculum in full
Exclude schools whose religious teaching it finds discriminatory
Pay religious schools for secular subjects like math, but not for religion
e: What Maine can’t do is exclude religious schools from the tuition benefit it chose to offer. States may keep their own public schools strictly secular.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: Even under Smith, which of these may government never do?
o: Take sides in religious controversies
Enforce drug laws against sacramental use
Require all businesses to close on Sundays
Draft conscientious objectors in wartime
e: Smith’s list also bars regulating belief as such, compelling affirmation, punishing doctrines as false, and status-based disabilities.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: In the casebook’s neutrality synthesis, which case is paired with Lukumi as the contrast, a law that is neutral and generally applicable?
o: Employment Division v. Smith
Tandon v. Newsom
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Carson v. Makin
e: Smith’s across-the-board drug ban had no exemptions. Lukumi’s ordinances exempted almost every secular killing.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: Which earlier case did Masterpiece cite for the principle that government can’t decide what is “offensive”?
o: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Cohen v. California
Wisconsin v. Yoder
e: Barnette: no official may prescribe what shall be orthodox. The commission had treated some objections as offensive and others as acceptable.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: What did Philadelphia’s foster care contract give the Commissioner in Fulton?
o: Sole discretion to grant exceptions to the policy
Power to certify foster parents without review
Authority to end any contract for any reason
A duty to refer every child to the nearest licensed agency
e: That discretion, not any exemption actually granted, defeated general applicability.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: In Tandon, which activities could exceed California’s three-household limit?
o: Hair salons, retail stores, movie theaters, and indoor restaurants
Only grocery stores, pharmacies, and hospitals
Outdoor protests and political rallies of any size
Schools, day-care centers, youth sports leagues, and summer camps
e: The majority used these comparators; the dissent said at-home secular gatherings, treated identically, were the right ones.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: In Trinity Lutheran, the first case in the funding trilogy with Carson, what was the church-run preschool denied?
o: A grant to resurface its playground
A tax-credit scholarship for its students
Tuition payments for rural families
A permit to expand its building
e: Excluding an otherwise eligible recipient solely because it was religious was “odious to our Constitution.”
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: A state bans alcohol for anyone under 21, with no exemptions of any kind. A 19-year-old wants to drink sacramental wine at services. Under the Free Exercise Clause alone, what result?
o: No exemption is required: the law is neutral and generally applicable
An exemption is required, because the sacramental use is sincere
An exemption is required unless the state proves a compelling interest
An exemption is required, because the law burdens worship itself
e: Smith controls. Only a statute could change the result: RFRA binds the federal government, and some states have their own versions.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: After a Buddhist group announces a ritual releasing captive birds, a town bans “releasing animals into the wild” but exempts hunting dogs, falconry, pest-control relocations, and wildlife rehabilitators. What result?
o: Strict scrutiny under Lukumi: the exemptions suggest a religious gerrymander
Rational basis under Smith, because the ban never mentions religion
No scrutiny, because releasing birds isn’t a recognized religious exercise at all
Intermediate scrutiny, because the ban regulates conduct, not belief
e: The timing and the exemptions leave comparable secular releases untouched, so the law isn’t neutral or generally applicable. It will likely fail strict scrutiny as underinclusive.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: A state board denies a Muslim artist’s request to decline certain religious imagery work. At the hearing a member calls her faith “a cover for bigotry,” and no one objects; a secular artist who refused similar work was cleared. Best answer?
o: The decision likely violates Free Exercise: hostile, unequal application
The decision is valid, because the state’s licensing law is neutral on its face
The decision is valid, because one member’s remarks can’t taint a board
She wins only if she proves the law was enacted to target her religion
e: Masterpiece: hostility in adjudication plus worse treatment than a comparable secular objector violates the Free Exercise Clause.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: A county contracts with private officiants for courthouse weddings. Each must perform every couple’s ceremony, but the clerk may grant “exceptions for good cause” at her discretion. A priest asks for an exception, and his contract is ended. What is the key first step?
o: The discretionary exceptions make the rule not generally applicable, so strict scrutiny applies
The rule is neutral, so Smith ends the case unless an exception was actually granted before
The priest must first show the clerk granted exceptions to secular officiants
The court must balance the priest’s burden against the couples’ dignity interests
e: Fulton: a formal system of individualized exemptions invites the government to decide which reasons are worthy, even if never used.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: A city caps religious services at 25 people for fire safety, but lets concert halls, gyms, and lecture halls of the same size hold 100, with the same exits and sprinklers. What result?
o: Strict scrutiny under Tandon: comparable secular activities are treated better
Rational basis under Smith: fire codes are neutral safety laws
No problem, so long as some secular venues, like nightclubs, are also capped at 25
Strict scrutiny only if the city admits it meant to single out worship
e: Comparability is judged by risk to the interest. Same size, same exits, same sprinklers: the city must show worship is riskier with the same precautions.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: A state gives grants to any private college to install solar panels but excludes colleges “affiliated with a church.” A church-affiliated college sues. What result?
o: Likely a Free Exercise violation: exclusion solely for religious character
Valid: the state may decline to fund religion to avoid Establishment concerns
Valid, if the state’s own constitution bars any aid to religious bodies
Valid, unless the college proves the state was hostile to its specific faith
e: The trilogy: once the state offers a generally available benefit, it can’t exclude otherwise eligible recipients because they are religious.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: In the Free Exercise checklist, what comes right after asking whether a sincere religious practice is burdened?
o: Is the law neutral and generally applicable?
Does the law survive strict scrutiny as applied?
Is a hybrid right involved?
Does RFRA apply to this government?
e: If the law is neutral and generally applicable, Smith denies an exemption unless Wrinkle 1 applies; otherwise strict scrutiny.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: Once strict scrutiny applies in a Free Exercise case, how often does the government win?
o: Almost never
About half the time
Usually
Always, in schools
e: That is why the fight is usually over whether the law is neutral and generally applicable.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: Which case illustrates “comparable secular activity favored” in the neutrality synthesis?
o: Tandon v. Newsom
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
Carson v. Makin
e: Fulton is the discretionary exemption system, Lukumi gerrymandered exemptions, and Carson exclusion from a benefit.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Which case illustrates a “discretionary exemption system” in the neutrality synthesis?
o: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Tandon v. Newsom
Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
e: Fulton’s Commissioner had sole discretion to grant exceptions, even though none had been granted.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Why did Mahmoud say little about the doctrinal basis for Wrinkle 1?
o: Wariness of unenumerated rights after Dobbs
The parties had waived the issue during the appeal
Yoder had already been overruled by Smith
The case was decided without oral argument
e: Smith had grounded Yoder in an unenumerated parental right, a basis the Court was reluctant to lean on.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The two wrinkles

q: Which case struck a moment of silence for prayer in public schools?
o: Wallace v. Jaffree
Engel v. Vitale
Abington v. Schempp
McCollum v. Board of Education
e: Engel struck nonmandatory prayer, Schempp Bible reading, and McCollum religious instruction.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: What did Engel v. Vitale strike down?
o: Nonmandatory prayer in public schools
Bible reading in public schools
Religious instruction in school buildings
Funding for religious schools
e: Public schools are policed most strictly because they are uniquely coercive and children are impressionable.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: Which sequence describes how religious-school funding doctrine has changed?
o: Exclusion permitted, then inclusion permitted, then inclusion required
Inclusion required, then inclusion permitted, then exclusion permitted again
Inclusion permitted, then exclusion required, then inclusion required
Exclusion required, then exclusion permitted, then inclusion permitted
e: The Lemon era allowed exclusion, Zelman (2002) permitted inclusion, and the trilogy (2017–2022) required it.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: What principle about unemployment benefits did Carson cite?
o: A state can’t deny benefits to someone fired for refusing to abandon her faith
A state may deny benefits to anyone who quits a job for any religious reason at all
Religious employers are exempt from paying into unemployment funds
Unemployment offices may not be located in religious buildings
e: The same principle that bars excluding religious schools from a benefit long protected claimants seeking unemployment benefits.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: Is RFRA part of constitutional law?
o: No; it is a statute that Congress can amend
Yes; it overruled Smith as a constitutional rule
Yes; it was ratified as an amendment in 1993
No; it is a regulation issued by the Justice Department
e: Because it is a statute, its reach depends on Congress’s power, which Boerne limited as to the states.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: What does RLUIPA cover?
o: Land use and institutionalized persons
Federal employment and military service
Public schools and state universities
Tax exemptions for religious groups
e: RLUIPA binds states and was unanimously upheld in Cutter v. Wilkinson.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: How are longstanding religious monuments and legislative prayers generally treated?
o: Allowed on historical grounds, like the Texas Ten Commandments monument
Struck under the endorsement test as government approval of one religion
Allowed only if the government pays for nothing related to them
Allowed only if they include symbols from every faith
e: Van Orden (2005) upheld a monument that had stood for 40 years. Public schools are stricter because students are impressionable.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: A city’s zoning code caps every building at 40 feet, with no exceptions or variances of any kind. A church wants a 60-foot steeple. Under the Free Exercise Clause, what result?
o: No exemption: the code is neutral and generally applicable
Strict scrutiny under Lukumi, because steeples are religious
Strict scrutiny under Fulton, because zoning involves permits
An exemption under Wrinkle 1, because the church runs a school
e: Under Smith, a truly across-the-board rule needs no exemption. A statute like RLUIPA, which covers land use, could change the answer.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: A state requires school vaccinations and allows medical exemptions but no religious ones. Religious parents sue. What is their strongest Free Exercise argument?
o: Medical exemptions favor a comparable secular reason, so Tandon applies
The law names no religion, so it must be a Lukumi-style religious gerrymander
Any law affecting children triggers Wrinkle 1 automatically
Vaccines are medical, so the Establishment Clause bars the requirement
e: Comparability is judged by risk: an unvaccinated child with a medical exemption poses the same risk as one with a religious objection. The state must then show the religious exemption is riskier.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: A state excludes religious schools from a voucher program, saying its own constitution requires stricter separation of church and state than the federal Constitution. Best response?
o: Wrinkle 2 doesn’t cover that: stricter separation isn’t a compelling interest
The exclusion is valid, because states may always add to the Establishment Clause
The exclusion is valid if the state also caps vouchers for secular schools
The exclusion is valid, because voucher money is public education money
e: Government may disfavor religion only when needed to avoid a federal Establishment Clause violation. Including religious schools through parents’ choice isn’t one (Zelman).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The two wrinkles

q: A public elementary school opens each day with a voluntary, teacher-led prayer; students may step into the hall. A parent sues. What result?
o: It violates the Establishment Clause, as in Engel
It is valid under Kennedy, because no student is forced to pray
It is valid, because history and tradition support legislative prayer too
It is valid, if students of every faith may take turns leading it
e: Engel struck nonmandatory school prayer. Teacher-led prayer to young children is government religious exercise, not private expression.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: A federal prison enforces a uniform no-beard rule for all inmates. A Muslim inmate wants to keep a short beard. Which law gives him his best claim?
o: RFRA, which binds the federal government and demands strict scrutiny
The Free Exercise Clause, which requires strict scrutiny for uniform rules
RLUIPA, which binds federal prisons and requires an exemption
None: Boerne struck down RFRA in every application
e: Boerne limited RFRA as to states and localities, but it still binds the federal government.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: In which case did the dissent disagree only about whether the challenged message was the government’s own speech?
o: Wooley v. Maynard
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Collin v. Smith
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
e: Wooley v. Maynard (1977). Government speech is a later topic in the course.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: In which case were the demonstrators represented by David Goldberger, a Jewish ACLU lawyer?
o: Collin v. Smith
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Brandenburg v. Ohio
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
e: Collin v. Smith (1978), the Skokie march case.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: In which case did the plaintiffs’ materials range from hard-core films to Yeats’s “Leda and the Swan” and works of Joyce and Lawrence?
o: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
United States v. Stevens
Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition
Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association
e: Hudnut (1985). It was unclear how Indianapolis would treat Ulysses or the Iliad.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: In which case did a statute aimed at “crush videos” turn out to reach hunting videos sold where hunting is restricted?
o: United States v. Stevens
United States v. Hansen
Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association
United States v. Alvarez
e: United States v. Stevens (2010). Read by its text, 18 U.S.C. § 48 required no cruelty.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: In which case did the defendant also falsely claim to have played for the Detroit Red Wings and married a starlet from Mexico?
o: United States v. Alvarez
United States v. Hansen
Counterman v. Colorado
Rice v. Paladin Enterprises, Inc.
e: United States v. Alvarez (2012). “Lying was his habit.”
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: In which case did a defendant whose own conduct was fraud argue that a statute was overbroad because it could reach advocacy?
o: United States v. Hansen
United States v. Stevens
United States v. Williams
United States v. Alvarez
e: United States v. Hansen (2023). Overbreadth lets a litigant with unprotected conduct assert others’ rights.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Which statement about Wooley v. Maynard is accurate?
o: Promoting state pride is ideological and can’t override the right not to carry it
The motto requirement stood, but drivers couldn’t be prosecuted for covering it
Only religious objectors may refuse to display a state’s official motto
It was decided under the Establishment Clause, because the objectors were Jehovah’s Witnesses
e: Religious plaintiffs, but a speech rationale that protects any objector. Vehicle identification was served by plate numbers.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: Which statement about Collin v. Smith is accurate?
o: The ordinances were content-based, not time, place, and manner rules
The ordinances were valid TPM rules because the march was short
The march was unprotected incitement because violence was widely expected
The ordinances failed only because the permit fee was too high
e: The village objected to who was marching, not when or where. It also conceded it expected no violence.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: Which statement about American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut is accurate?
o: Material showing women as equals was lawful; material showing subordination was banned
The ordinance banned all sexually explicit material, however it portrayed women or men
The ordinance tracked the Miller test, so it was upheld as an obscenity law
The court rejected the city’s claim that such depictions cause any harm at all
e: Treating one side differently from the other is viewpoint discrimination, which is what doomed the ordinance.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: Which statement about United States v. Stevens is accurate?
o: It refused to make depictions of animal cruelty a new unprotected category
It held that crush videos are protected speech in every possible form
It upheld the law as applied but struck it as to hunting videos
It upheld the law as applied to dogfights but struck it as to hunting videos
e: Stevens left open a statute limited to crush videos or extreme cruelty.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: Which statement about United States v. Alvarez is accurate?
o: The Medal’s integrity was compelling, but the Act wasn’t actually necessary
The Medal’s integrity was too weak an interest to count as compelling
The Act fell because Alvarez sought money and other benefits through his lie
The Act was upheld as applied to statements made at public meetings
e: There was no evidence the lies diluted the Medal, and counterspeech worked.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: Which statement about United States v. Hansen is accurate?
o: Read as solicitation and facilitation, the law’s protected applications were fanciful
It struck the law because it reached ordinary advocacy on behalf of noncitizens and their families
It held fraud aimed at noncitizens is protected speech under the First Amendment
It held overbreadth challenges unavailable to defendants in criminal cases
e: Without a lopsided ratio of realistic protected applications, the law survived.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Why did it matter in Wooley that driving is a virtual necessity?
o: Drivers couldn’t avoid carrying the state’s message on their own cars
Driving is a privilege, so the state could attach whatever conditions it chose
Necessity meant the state had to supply plates free of charge
It made the motto the drivers’ own speech rather than the state’s
e: The car became a “mobile billboard” for the state’s ideological message.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: Which exceptions to the ban on content regulation did Collin recognize, drawing on Mosley?
o: Obscenity, fighting words, libel, and narrow imminent danger
Hate speech, group libel, and symbols of genocide
Profanity, indecency, and offensive symbols such as swastikas
Any speech that causes a minority psychic trauma
e: Burger’s Mosley concurrence listed these. The village’s ordinances fit none of them.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: Why did Hudnut say the city’s rationale couldn’t be contained?
o: Any rationale for silencing harmful views couldn’t stay limited to sex
The city admitted it planned to extend the ordinance to violent films
The Supreme Court had already approved a broader group-libel law
Seditious libel is unprotected, so the rationale already reached political speech
e: Speech has been an ally of those seeking change. Seditious libel is protected unless the danger is grave and imminent.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: Why didn’t § 48’s exception for serious value save it in Stevens?
o: Its terms didn’t reliably cover hunting videos and other lawful material
Courts never consider statutory exceptions when they analyze overbreadth
Serious value is a test only for obscenity, never for other speech
Congress had repealed the exception before the prosecution began
e: Lawful applications, like hunting videos, dwarfed the crush and dogfight market, so the ratio was lopsided.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: What did Alvarez fear would follow from upholding the Stolen Valor Act?
o: Government could list subjects about which lies are crimes
Government could ban all paid political advertising before elections
Government could license speakers at public meetings
Government could prosecute opinions as false facts
e: The Act reached lies anywhere, even whispered at home, and targeted falsity and nothing more.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: Which principle did Hansen invoke for choosing a constitutional reading of a statute?
o: The Ashwander principle of constitutional avoidance
The Salerno rule for ordinary facial challenges
The Mosley principle against content regulation
The Giboney rule for speech integral to criminal conduct
e: If a statute can fairly be read two ways, choose the constitutional reading; courts seek harmony, not collision.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Which interests did New Hampshire offer for its motto requirement in Wooley?
o: Identifying vehicles and promoting state pride and history
Traffic safety and reducing the theft of license plates from parked cars
Raising revenue and deterring drunk driving
Wartime unity and civic education of students
e: Identification could be done with plate numbers, so it wasn’t narrowly tailored. Pride and history were ideological.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: What did the march permit in Collin allow?
o: 30 to 50 uniformed marchers, single file, for half an hour, with no speeches
A full-day rally in the village park with amplified speeches, music, and handbills
A march through residential streets ending at a synagogue
A permanent display of party flags outside Village Hall
e: The placards included “Free Speech for White America.” The village still couldn’t stop it for its content.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: Which drafter of the Hudnut ordinance asked, “if a woman is subjected, why should it matter that the work has other value?”
o: Catharine MacKinnon
Kathleen M. Sullivan
Thomas Emerson
Greg Garre
e: The drafters saw the ordinance’s departures from Miller as virtues; the court saw viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: How would the dissent in Stevens have handled § 48?
o: Read the statute narrowly
Struck it as unconstitutionally vague
Upheld it as an obscenity law
Remanded for more facts
e: The majority declined to rewrite the statute, since the avoidance canon can’t override clear text.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: As the outline explains with Alvarez, what does “concurring in the judgment” mean?
o: Agreeing with the result but not the reasoning
Agreeing with the reasoning but not the result
Joining every part of the main opinion without reservation
Dissenting from part of the judgment
e: A plurality is fewer than five Justices joining the reasoning, so it usually isn’t binding.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: What limit does the avoidance canon have, as Hansen notes?
o: It can’t override clear statutory text
It applies only to federal criminal statutes
It applies only in civil cases
It needs the government’s consent
e: That is why Stevens read § 48 by its ordinary meaning instead of narrowing it.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: A state requires every storefront business to display a state-issued window poster reading “Proud to Support Our State’s Values.” A shop owner refuses. What result?
o: Unconstitutional compelled speech under Wooley
Valid, because businesses get less protection than drivers
Valid, as a compelled factual commercial disclosure
Valid, because most residents approve of the message
e: The state may not make a person display its ideological message on private property for the public to see.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: A town where a mass shooting occurred denies a parade permit to a group that wants to march on a public street with signs praising the shooter’s ideology, citing residents’ trauma. No violence is expected. What result?
o: The denial is unconstitutional: content-based, with no captive audience or expected violence
The denial is valid: psychic trauma to survivors is a compelling interest that justifies it
The denial is valid: praising a shooter’s ideology is incitement under Brandenburg
The denial is valid: residents are a captive audience on their own town’s streets
e: Collin: government may not ban a peaceful demonstration because of its message, however painful.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: A state bans video games that “portray immigrants as criminals,” citing studies that such games increase discrimination. What result under Hudnut?
o: Unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination, even if the harm is real
Valid, if the studies prove the games cause discrimination
Valid, because video games are entertainment rather than political speech
Valid, because it reaches only one disfavored message
e: Hudnut accepted that the speech caused harm and still struck the ordinance: harm through ideas only proves speech’s power.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: A state bans selling videos depicting “the killing of any wild animal,” aiming at poaching videos. Hunting shows are popular there, and a hunting-show producer challenges the law. What result?
o: Likely facially overbroad: lawful hunting videos dwarf the poaching market
Valid, because depictions of animal killing are an unprotected category of speech
Valid, because the state promises to prosecute only poaching videos
Valid, because the law has some legitimate applications to poaching
e: Stevens: a law that reaches a substantial amount of protected speech relative to its legitimate sweep is facially invalid.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: A state makes it a crime to falsely claim, anywhere, to hold a college degree. A man falsely claims a law degree at a dinner party and gains nothing. What result?
o: Likely unconstitutional under Alvarez: falsity alone, with no cognizable harm
Valid: false statements are a historically unprotected category of speech
Valid: the interest in degree integrity is compelling, so the law is necessary
Valid: the lie was made in a private home, where speech gets less protection
e: Lies tied to legally cognizable harm, like fraud to get a job, can be punished. Falsity alone can’t.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: A statute bars “aiding or encouraging” tax evasion. A blogger who writes that the income tax is unconstitutional and urges readers to stop paying is charged. Under Hansen’s approach, what should the court do first?
o: Read the terms as solicitation and facilitation of specific unlawful acts
Strike the statute as overbroad because it could reach the blog post
Uphold the conviction because tax evasion is a serious federal crime
Apply strict scrutiny, because the statute regulates speech based on its content
e: Read as criminal-law terms of art, the statute reaches solicitation and facilitation of specific unlawful acts, not general advocacy.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Why is false, heinous, or harmful speech often protected?
o: Officials and courts can’t be trusted to separate truth from falsity
Such speech always has some political value that listeners deserve to hear
The Framers protected harmful speech expressly in the text
Only private parties may sue over harmful speech
e: The same distrust explains the preference for bright lines and the refusal to add unprotected categories.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: Which of these is NOT a step on the speech checklist?
o: Is the speaker a citizen?
Is there government action?
Is it compelled speech?
Is the law content-based?
e: The checklist also asks whether the speech fits a narrow historical category and whether the law is overbroad or vague.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: Which case established compelled-speech doctrine in the course materials?
o: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Wooley v. Maynard
Collin v. Smith
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
e: Wooley extended Barnette from saluting a flag to passively displaying a motto.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Compelled speech

q: Which is the worst form of content discrimination?
o: Viewpoint discrimination
Subject-matter restrictions
Time, place, and manner limits
Secondary-effects zoning
e: Banning only pro-legalization publications, or rejecting “FCANCER” while allowing other plates, are examples.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: Classify a ban on “publications advocating marijuana legalization.”
o: Viewpoint-based
Content-neutral
Unprotected incitement
A secondary-effects rule
e: It silences one side of a debate, so it is the worst form of content regulation and gets strict scrutiny.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: What did Mosley, as quoted in Collin, say government has no power to do?
o: Restrict expression because of its message, ideas, subject, or content
Regulate the time, place, or manner of any demonstration on a public street
Require permits for marches on public streets
Protect listeners in their homes from unwanted speech
e: Debate must be “uninhibited, robust, and wide-open” (NYT v. Sullivan).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: Which case does the outline list as the key case for fraud as unprotected speech?
o: Virginia Board of Pharmacy (1976)
Watts v. United States
Giboney v. Empire Storage & Ice Co.
Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire
e: Alvarez distinguished lies with legally cognizable harm, like fraud, from falsity alone.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: Which category’s key case is Watts v. United States?
o: True threats
Fighting words
Incitement
Obscenity
e: Counterman later added the recklessness requirement for true threats.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: Why is overbreadth called “strong medicine”?
o: It invalidates a law that has lawful applications
It requires the defendant to prove actual chilling
It applies only to speech of the highest value
It lets courts rewrite statutes on their own
e: That is why Hansen required realistic protected applications and a lopsided ratio.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q: A public school bans black armbands worn to protest a war, calling them “clothing, not speech.” What is the first answer to the school’s argument?
o: Symbolic acts like armbands are speech under the First Amendment
The school is right: clothing is conduct the school may regulate freely
The school is right unless the armband includes written words
Armbands are speech only if worn outside school grounds
e: Speech includes symbolic acts: armbands, flags, crosses, parades, and picketing. The analysis then moves to content and justification.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: A city requires restaurants to post calorie counts on menus. A restaurant claims compelled speech. Likely result?
o: Valid: compelled factual commercial disclosures are allowed
Invalid under Wooley: the owner can’t be made to carry any message
Invalid under Barnette: the owner must affirm a belief about nutrition
Valid only if customers can easily cover the numbers
e: Compelled commercial disclosures like nutrition labels and drug side effects are the main exception (Ch. 8).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Compelled speech

q: A city bans all yard signs except real-estate signs and signs supporting its “Clean Streets” campaign. A resident wants an anti-campaign sign. How should the ban be classified?
o: Viewpoint-based as to the campaign signs, so strict scrutiny applies
Content-neutral, because it limits where every sign may be placed in the city
A time, place, and manner rule, because signs are on private yards
Valid, because the city’s own campaign is government speech
e: Allowing signs for the campaign but not against it favors one side, the worst form of content regulation.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: A state creates a new crime: selling “extremely gory” videos of real human violence. It argues the videos have little value and cause real harm. What result?
o: Likely invalid: courts don’t create new categories by balancing value and harm
Valid: speech of little value is unprotected under the categorical approach to speech
Valid: Ferber allows bans whenever the content shows real harm
Valid: the videos are obscene because they are deeply offensive
e: Stevens and Brown: the First Amendment already reflects the people’s cost-benefit judgment, and violence isn’t a category.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: A man convicted under a true-threats statute argues it is overbroad because a prosecutor could, in theory, charge someone for a joke. What does he need to show?
o: Realistic protected applications, substantial relative to its legitimate sweep
At least one hypothetical application to protected speech, however unlikely it may be
That his own statement was protected speech rather than a true threat
That the statute has no valid applications to real threats at all
e: Hansen: the unconstitutional applications must be realistic, not fanciful, and the ratio lopsided.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q: Which case required a clear and present danger of a serious evil “far above public inconvenience, annoyance, or unrest”?
o: Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Brandenburg v. Ohio
Whitney v. California
New York Times Co. v. United States
e: Terminiello v. City of Chicago (1949), from the middle era of incitement doctrine.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello v. City of Chicago

q: In which case was the only audience Klan members and the journalists they invited?
o: Brandenburg v. Ohio
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Collin v. Smith
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
e: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969). The speech was filmed at a farm rally.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg v. Ohio

q: In which case did a state court construe an ordinance to reach only fighting words, yet the Supreme Court struck it anyway?
o: R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
Cohen v. California
Collin v. Smith
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
e: R.A.V. (1992). Even limited to fighting words, the ordinance picked out race, color, creed, religion, and gender.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul

q: Which 1931 case is the foundation of the heavy presumption against prior restraints?
o: Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson
New York Times Co. v. United States
Whitney v. California
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
e: Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931). Bantam Books later restated the heavy presumption.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson

q: In which case did the Court grant cert on June 25, hear argument June 26, and rule June 30?
o: New York Times Co. v. United States
Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson
Brandenburg v. Ohio
Cohen v. California
e: The Pentagon Papers case (1971). The dissent said the issues were hard and the decision too rushed.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — New York Times Co. v. United States

q: Which statement about Terminiello v. City of Chicago is accurate?
o: It reversed because the instruction let the jury convict for speech that invited dispute
It reversed because the speech was a sermon, protected by the Free Exercise Clause instead
It affirmed because the crowd outside actually turned violent
It adopted Brandenburg’s incitement test twenty years early
e: The facts sounded like incitement, but the breach-of-the-peace instruction swept in protected speech.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello v. City of Chicago

q: Which statement about Brandenburg v. Ohio is accurate?
o: Ohio’s law punished mere advocacy, with no intent, imminence, or likelihood
Ohio’s law was valid on its face but was misapplied to this particular speaker
The conviction stood because armed men burned a cross at the rally
Klan speech counts as fighting words whenever a cross is burned
e: The statute was unconstitutional on its face, and Whitney’s majority was overruled.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg v. Ohio

q: Which statement about R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul is accurate?
o: The ordinance was facially invalid even assuming it reached only fighting words
The cross burning was protected speech that no law of any kind could ever punish
The ordinance was valid, but the teenagers’ conduct fell outside it
Fighting words are now fully protected speech like any other
e: Other laws, like trespass or arson, could still reach the conduct. The problem was selective regulation within a category.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul

q: Which statement about Near v. Minnesota is accurate?
o: Its wartime examples were dicta; the injunction itself was reversed
It upheld the injunction because the articles were defamatory
It held prior restraints forbidden in every possible circumstance, even war
It held the press may be punished only by advance restraint
e: Protection from prior restraint isn’t absolute, but the only suggested exception has never been applied.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson

q: Which statement about New York Times Co. v. United States is accurate?
o: Publication was restrained for 15 days before the Court denied the injunctions
The Court allowed a brief injunction while classified papers were reviewed by judges
The Court held that the study had never been properly classified
The Court held the Espionage Act authorized the injunctions
e: A general claim of harm to national security didn’t carry the government’s heavy burden.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — New York Times Co. v. United States

q: Where does Terminiello fit in the history of incitement doctrine?
o: The 1949–51 era: clear and present danger of a serious evil
The 1919–27 era: bad tendency, used to punish wartime dissidents
The modern era: intent, imminence, and likelihood
The fighting-words era begun by Chaplinsky
